cards.front: What transport protocol provides reliable, ordered delivery of data?
cards.back: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) uses acknowledgements, sequencing, and retransmission to guarantee reliable, ordered delivery.

cards.front: What transport protocol is connectionless and does not guarantee delivery?
cards.back: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) sends datagrams without establishing a connection, trading reliability for lower latency.

cards.front: What does DNS stand for and what does it do?
cards.back: Domain Name System. It translates human-readable domain names like example.com into IP addresses that computers use to route traffic.

cards.front: What does DHCP do on a network?
cards.back: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, gateways, and DNS servers to devices joining a network.
A numerical label (e.g. 192.168.1.1 for IPv4 or 2001:db8::1 for IPv6) assigned to each device on a network, used to identify and route packets.

cards.front: What is a subnet mask used for?
cards.back: A subnet mask (e.g. 255.255.255.0) divides an IP address into a network portion and a host portion, defining which addresses are on the same local network.

cards.front: What is the key difference between a router and a switch?
cards.back: A switch forwards frames within a single local network using MAC addresses. A router forwards packets between different networks using IP addresses.

cards.front: What is the main difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
cards.back: HTTPS adds TLS/SSL encryption on top of HTTP, so data in transit is encrypted and the server's identity is verified by a certificate.

cards.front: What are well-known port numbers for HTTP and HTTPS?
cards.back: HTTP uses port 80 by default. HTTPS uses port 443 by default. Ports below 1024 are considered well-known or system ports.
Latency is the time it takes for a packet to travel from source to destination. It is commonly measured as round-trip time (RTT) in milliseconds.
